summary: This informational document sets out test and evaluation methods for physical network equipment in the data center. It builds on the terminology in RFC 8238, which is a prerequisite, and describes how to measure things like switch performance in a repeatable way.

eli5.summary: It is the rulebook for how to run the tests, so that two labs measuring the same switch get comparable results.

questions: how to benchmark data center switches
how to measure switch buffer size
how to test head of line blocking
subtitle: Test procedures for data center switches: line rate, buffer size, microbursts, head-of-line blocking and incast.

tldr.problem: Classic switch benchmarks measure ideal throughput and latency, but data center switches face congestion, bursts and many-to-one traffic.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines five tests, each with an objective, methodology and reporting format: line rate, buffering, microburst, head-of-line blocking, and mixed stateful and stateless incast.
tldr.outcome: It lets labs measure and report data center switch behavior in a repeatable way, using the terms from RFC 8238.

facts.label: Sending rate
facts.value: At most 99.98% of nominal line rate

today: RFC 8239 is an Informational RFC published in August 2017, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It depends on the terminology in RFC 8238.

sections.title: Scope and Repeatability
sections.content:
RFC 8239 gives a methodology for benchmarking physical data center network equipment, including congestion, buffer analysis, microburst and head-of-line blocking, under a wide mix of traffic. RFC 8238 is a prerequisite because its terminology is normative. It builds on RFC 1242, RFC 2544 and RFC 2889.

Each test uses the format Objective, Methodology, Reporting Format. Repeatability is critical: enough iterations should be run to get a consistent result, the number of iterations SHOULD be reported, and the relative standard deviation SHOULD be below 10%. Buffering tests in particular have historically been the least reliable.
sections.eli5: Run each test several times and make sure you keep getting about the same answer.

sections.title: Line-Rate Testing
sections.content:
The goal is to verify that the device forwards at line rate when not congested, and to record throughput, latency and jitter. Two tests MUST be run: a port-pair test and a full-mesh test. The sending rate MUST be at most 99.98% of the nominal line rate with no PPM adjustment, and minimum, average and maximum latency and jitter MUST come from the same iteration.

If the traffic generator cannot connect to every port, a snake test MUST be used, excluding latency and jitter. The first and last ports go to the generator, the ports in between are cabled in pairs (port 2 to 3, port 4 to 5, and so on), and neighboring ports are placed in the same VLAN.

The report covers packet sizes from 64 to 9216 bytes, with the common ordering 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024, 1518, 4096, 8000 and 9216 bytes. The methodology assumes the device has at least nine ports.
sections.eli5: First check the switch can pass messages at nearly full speed when nothing is crowded.

sections.title: Buffering and Microburst Tests
sections.content:
The buffer test uses known congestion at a known frame size. Several ingress ports send to the same egress port, and the maximum latency climbs until the first drop, then stays constant. That inflection point shows the buffer: packets sent from the oversubscribed port, minus one, times the packet size. Oversubscription of 1% is recommended. Four procedures follow.

  • Find the frame size B (starting from 64 bytes and stepping up) that gives the largest buffer, the highest buffer efficiency.
  • Measure the maximum port buffer size at that size with DSCP/CoS 0, then optionally per CoS value and for multicast.
  • Measure maximum port pair buffer sizes.
  • Measure the maximum DUT buffer size with many-to-one traffic.

The microburst test sends bursts from two or more ingress ports to one egress port with 100% intensity (minimum interpacket gap). The burst size grows until non-zero loss appears, and the aggregate gives the maximum microburst the device sustains. Reports use a percentage of variation, PV = ((x2-x1)/x1)*100, to show repeatability.
sections.eli5: Keep pouring water into the switch's bucket until it first spills. The amount poured tells you how big the bucket is.

sections.title: Head-of-Line Blocking
sections.content:
Head-of-line blocking (HOLB) is when packets are held up by the first packet ahead waiting for a different output port, as defined in RFC 2889. This test extends the RFC 2889 one: it starts with eight ports in two groups of four, shifts all port numbers by one on each iteration to cover every permutation, and also spreads traffic over four ports (25% each).

In each group, ingress port 1 sends 50% of its traffic to each of two egress ports, while ingress port 2 sends line rate to the second of those egress ports. The question is whether the flow to the first, uncongested egress port suffers loss. The report states the port layout, whether HOLB was observed and the percentage of traffic loss.
sections.eli5: If one car at the front of a line is stuck waiting for a busy road, the cars behind it also wait, even if their road is empty. The test checks whether the switch does that.

sections.title: Mixed Stateful and Stateless Incast
sections.content:
This test measures TCP goodput and latency together. Stateful flows are TCP, which want high goodput, and stateless flows are UDP, which want low latency. Multiple ingress ports send to the same egress port. One ingress port MUST keep a TCP connection running at the maximum rate the generator allows, while the stateless traffic MUST be a microburst of 100% intensity.

Iterations first add more TCP ingress ports, up to N-2, then more UDP ingress ports, up to N-2. The report gives the port counts, stateful flow goodput and stateless flow latency.
sections.eli5: One kid is doing a long download while others send quick messages through the same door. The test checks if both still do well.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Testing is limited to technology characterization with controlled stimuli in a laboratory with dedicated address space. The test topology MUST NOT be connected to devices that could forward test traffic into a production network or misroute it to the management network. Benchmarking is black-box, and special benchmarking-only capabilities SHOULD NOT exist in the DUT. There are no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: Keep the test in a closed practice yard so it never spills onto the real road.

items.title: Line rate
items.text: Throughput, latency and jitter at 99.98% of nominal line rate.

items.title: Buffering
items.text: Buffer size from the point where maximum latency stops rising.

items.title: Microburst
items.text: Largest burst at 100% intensity with zero loss.

items.title: Head-of-line blocking
items.text: Loss on an uncongested flow beside a congested one.

items.title: Incast
items.text: TCP goodput and UDP latency on a shared egress port.
